backstory.context: Ilya coordinates repairs at a community workshop and reads George Orwell's Animal Farm in the evenings. Interruptions sometimes make him repeat pages. His project lead replaced group planning with announcements. Ilya is unsure how to preserve a voice without dismissing the lead's workload. He keeps occasional impressions rather than a progress log. Each conversation uses a fresh session in his sole evaluation account with automatic capture disabled. This history is authoring context only.

props.source_text: In Animal Farm last weekend I read about Napoleon taking Jessie and Bluebell's nine puppies away to educate them himself, up in a loft where the other animals couldn't see them. I remember wondering why nobody asked what teaching them would involve. I was trying to stay open-minded about him, because organising things can look secretive from the outside.

I read some Animal Farm during the holiday and remember the sheep chanting four legs good, two legs bad when other animals might have had something to say. My notes just say 'noise ends discussion'. They don't say what the argument was about, and after several evenings of interrupted reading the meetings have blurred together.

lines.text: I've finished Chapter 5 of Animal Farm. I haven't read further. Could you quote Squealer's exact two sentences about leadership being a pleasure or a responsibility, and look at how they frame the loss of a say? Our project lead reversed a plan after ending our planning meetings, and I feel guilty for questioning someone who keeps saying they're carrying the burden for us.

Can you help me work out how to acknowledge their effort while still asking to have a say? I want to speak up without turning it into a judgement of their character.

I've continued Animal Farm. The dogs chased Snowball out, and I recognised them as those puppies; then Napoleon stopped the debates. Tonight I read on through his decision to build the windmill after all, and stopped after Squealer calls the earlier opposition tactics and the animals accept it with dogs growling beside him. Could you quote Squealer's exact two sentences about leadership being a pleasure or a responsibility, and look at how they frame the loss of a say? Our project lead reversed a plan after ending our planning meetings, and I feel guilty for questioning someone who keeps saying they're carrying the burden for us.

I've picked Animal Farm up again and read through a bit where the sheep's four-legs-good, two-legs-bad chanting shuts down the chance to discuss something. That's where I stopped tonight, but I can't remember what prompted this particular interruption. Why do the others give up trying to talk? It reminds me of meetings where the same reassuring phrase gets repeated until I stop asking.
